/status.about: Whether LunarLink is up, which build is running and whether a moon is loaded. It answers at the main menu too, so a script can wait on it.
/status.use: The first call of any script: wait until it answers with `world: true` before doing anything else, and compare `version` with `installed-version` to know whether the game is running the build you installed.
notes: `version` is the core's build stamp; `./build.sh --install` writes the same stamp to `BepInEx/plugins/LunarLink/installed-version`. If they differ, restart the game.
`world`: a moon is loaded. `time`: game seconds. `queued`: requests waiting for a frame. `served`: requests answered since start. `frames`: frames since start.

/support.about: Write a support file, `BepInEx/lunarlink-support-<date-time>.zip`, to attach to a bug report: what failed, the errors from the logs of this run and the previous one, the plugins and the settings, with names, Steam ids, the user name, LAN addresses and the access key blanked out.
/support.use: When something goes wrong (a plugin fails, crashes or doesn't load, the game freezes): open it in a browser and attach the zip it names to a GitHub issue. It answers at the main menu, while a module is broken, and while the game is frozen.
notes: A browser gets a short page instead of JSON: where the file is, and what it found.

In the zip: `summary.txt` (what looks wrong first, then the setup and the moment), `plugins/` (hot plugins, BepInEx plugins and their dependency errors, every DLL with its date and hash, the updater), `logs/` and `previous-run/` (errors with the lines round them, the start and end of the BepInEx, game and LunarLink logs, any freeze), `crashes/` (Unity's crash reports) and `config/`.
LunarLink keeps a copy of the BepInEx log as the game runs (`plugins/LunarLink/support/`), so a crashed run's log is still in the file after a restart. The last five support files are kept.
F9's **Support file** button does the same.

/hot/list.about: Every DLL in `BepInEx/hot/`: its state, the loaded build's time, whether a newer build is on disk, its error, leftovers and the old copies still in memory.
/hot/list.use: See whether your plugins are running, which failed and why, and whether a newer build is waiting on disk. With `?gc=1`, check that reloads don't pile up old copies in memory (`oldCopiesAlive` should stay 0 or 1).
params: Collect garbage first (three passes), so `oldCopiesAlive` is exact. A short hitch
/hot/list.answer:
{
 "dir": "C:\\Games\\Moon Sweepers\\BepInEx\\hot",
 "bridges": {
  "kept": 114,
  "freed": 0,
  "typesFreed": 0,
  "waiting": 0,
  "problem": null
 },
 "plugins": [
  {
   "name": "LunarLink.Api",
   "state": "running",
   "built": "2026-11-13 15:34:04",
   "error": null,
   "loads": 1,
   "boot": false,
   "newerOnDisk": false,
   "leftovers": [],
   "oldCopiesAlive": 0,
   "oldCopies": 0
  },
  {
   "name": "LunarLink.Perf",
   "state": "running",
   "built": "2026-11-13 15:34:04",
   "error": null,

   "boot": false,
   "newerOnDisk": false,
   "leftovers": [],
   "oldCopiesAlive": 0,
   "oldCopies": 0
  }
 ]
}
notes: `state`: `running`, `loaded` (waiting for a moon), `disabled` or `failed` (with `error`).
`boot`: `false` (no `Boot()`), `"done"`, or `"restart to boot"` when it was turned on after game start.
`leftovers`: Harmony patches still in after its last `Stop()`, which LunarLink took out.
`bridges`: the clean-up of Il2CppInterop and Harmony caches that frees old copies.

/hot/reload.about: Reload a hot plugin from the build on disk now: the old copy's `Stop()`, then the new copy's `Start(state)` with what it handed over. Turns the plugin on if it was off.
/hot/reload.use: The heart of the edit-build-reload loop: after building a plugin into `BepInEx/hot/`, call this and the game runs the new code within a frame. `./build.sh --hot` calls it for you; `?all=1` picks up everything you rebuilt.
params: The plugin's name: its DLL's name without `.dll`, as `/hot/list` shows it
Instead of `name`: reload every enabled plugin with a newer build on disk
errors: `"ok": false` with the reason in `plugin.error`: it didn't load, or its `Start` threw; it's unloaded again
notes: With `all=1` the answer is `{"ok":true,"ms":40,"reloaded":[ ...one entry per plugin... ]}`.
`./build.sh --hot <Name>` builds, copies and calls this for you.

/hot/enable.about: Load and start a hot plugin, and remember in `hot.json` that it's on.
/hot/enable.use: Turn on a plugin you dropped into `BepInEx/hot/` (new DLLs start off), or one you turned off. It's remembered across restarts.
params: The plugin's name, as `/hot/list` shows it
notes: Before a moon is loaded the plugin is `loaded` and starts once one is.

/hot/disable.about: Stop a hot plugin and unload it from memory, and remember in `hot.json` that it's off. Its code, patches and endpoints leave the game; no restart.
/hot/disable.use: Take a plugin out of the game completely while it runs: its code, patches and endpoints leave memory. Handy to rule a plugin out when hunting a problem, without restarting.
params: The plugin's name, as `/hot/list` shows it
notes: Disabling `LunarLink.Api` takes every game endpoint with it; `/status` and `/hot/*` stay, so you can turn it back on.

/hot/rescan.about: Look at `BepInEx/hot/` again: DLLs added since are listed (and stay off until enabled), DLLs removed are stopped and unloaded.
/hot/rescan.use: After copying DLLs into or out of `BepInEx/hot/` by hand, make LunarLink notice them without restarting.

/structures.about: Every structure in the world: id, kind, position, rotation, what it stands on and what it stores. Filter it: on a big base the full list is thousands of entries.
/structures.use: Find what's built where: everything near a point (`x,y,z,r`), only one kind (`kind=99`: the robots), or only what a script just built (`since=`). Almost every build or clean-up script starts here.
params: A world point (the moon's centre is 0,0,0; its surface is about 2000 m out)
Only within this many metres of the point
Only ids above this one: what was just built
notes: `yaw` and `q`: rotation as an angle and as a quaternion. `support`: the id it stands on (0 for the ground).
`/kinds` names the kinds.

/belts.about: Every belt piece: id, start and end points with their directions, and length.
/belts.use: Every belt with its ends and directions: for mapping a base's lines, finding a belt to extend or remove, or checking a script's belts.

/stations.about: The stations (the big depots): index, name, position and their conveyor intake sockets.
/stations.use: Where the stations are and their conveyor intake sockets: the points to run belts into.

/stations/shape.about: Every collider of a station as the 8 corners of its box: what's solid there.
/stations/shape.use: The solid parts of a station as boxes: what a building or belt next to it must not overlap.

/stations/footprint.about: Where a station's building really is: rays straight down onto its colliders on a grid, as world points.
/stations/footprint.use: Where a station's building really stands on the ground, as points, so a script can plan floors and belts right up to it without guessing from its centre.

/terrain.about: Ground heights on a square grid round a point, in the point's own frame: east, north and up from the moon's centre.
/terrain.use: The ground's height on a grid round a point, before building: to find flat spots, plan posts and raised floors over slopes, or check a belt's slope.
params: Half the square's side in metres (5 to 400)
notes: `h`: `n` x `n` heights in metres relative to the centre, row by row from north to south, each row west to east.

/canisters.about: Capsules near a point (dust, sand, stone): cargo, kilograms, whether each is riding a belt or carried; and totals for the whole moon.
/canisters.use: See capsules near a point (cargo, weight, riding a belt or lying loose) and the moon's totals: whether a line is moving, or where capsules pile up.
params: A world point (the moon's centre is 0,0,0; its surface is about 2000 m out)
notes: `total`: dropped capsules on the moon. `riding`: capsules on belts.

/kinds.about: Structure kinds: the ones standing in the world, or with `all=1` every kind the game defines. Name, prefab, price, footprint, height, reach and ports.
/kinds.use: The names, prices, footprints, heights and ports of every structure kind: what a build script needs to choose and place pieces. `all=1` includes kinds not yet built.
params: Every kind the game defines, not only those standing

/kit.about: The conveyor kit's limits: shortest and longest belt, tightest radius, steepest slope, lowest and highest point, and the price per metre.
/kit.use: The belt rules: shortest and longest belt, tightest turn, steepest slope, height limits, price per metre. Check them before planning a route.

/specs.about: Machine recipes and belt numbers: batch sizes, cycle times, power, slots, belt speed and spacing.
/specs.use: Machine recipes and belt numbers (batch sizes, cycle times, power, belt speed): for working out how many machines a line needs.

/sun.about: The sun: its direction, its height in degrees, the lunar day's length and the clock.
/sun.use: Where the sun is and the time of the lunar day: plan solar panels, or time something for daylight.

/moon.about: The cleaned share of the moon, as the map screen shows it.
/moon.use: How much of the moon is clean, as the map screen shows it: a progress number for scripts or overlays.
notes: `labels` is empty until the map screen has been opened once.

/dust/regions.about: Every dust region not yet complete: its index, centre direction, dust left and dust it started with.
/dust/regions.use: Which regions of the moon still have dust, and how much: send robots or a cleaning run where it's needed. Large: filter it in your script.
notes: **Large:** each entry is `[index, x, y, z, left, started]`, and a fresh moon has over 150,000 (about 6 MB).
`count`: regions on the moon; `left`: regions not complete.

/dust/geometry.about: Writes every region centre, and the centre of each chunk file named in `chunk_names.txt`, to `dust_geometry.json` in `BepInEx/plugins/LunarLink/`, for editing the save's dust offline.
/dust/geometry.use: For save editing: writes the region and chunk-file centres to a file, to edit the save's dust offline.
notes: A GET that writes a file (it changes nothing in the game).

/production.about: Every production machine (pressure chambers and stone presses): cycles done, progress, power, the game's status text and what each input and output slot holds.
/production.use: A full report of every press and chamber: what's running, what's starved of dust or sand, what's waiting on power. Use `/base/health` first to find a problem; then this to look at the machines involved.
notes: `kind`: 96 pressure chamber, 97 stone press (see `/specs`).
`status`, `flow`, `powerStatus`: the game's own text when it's waiting or stuck; empty when it's fine.
`lastCycle`, `lastInput`: game time of the last finished cycle and the last capsule in.
On a big base this is long (hundreds of machines): use `/base/health` to find problems.

/catchers.about: Every capsule catcher: kilograms stored, whether it's full and whether its outlet works.
/catchers.use: See which capsule catchers are full and whether their outlets move capsules on: a full catcher with a dead outlet is a base that has stopped.
notes: `storeKg`: what a catcher holds before it counts as full.
`outfeed`: its outlet is connected and moving capsules on.

/power.about: The solar panel types, and every power grid: panels, machines, supply, demand, use, satisfaction and battery charge.
/power.use: Check each solar grid has enough supply for its machines, and how much battery is left for the night.
notes: `satisfaction`: the share of demand met (1 = all).
`storedKwh` / `capacityKwh`: the grid's batteries.

/base/health.about: Is the base round a point working? Lists only real problems: machines the game says are stuck (with its reason), catchers with a dead outlet, robots docked there that aren't cleaning, and power grids short anywhere. Idle machines are only counted.
/base/health.use: One call answers "is this base working?": it lists only real problems (stuck machines with the game's reason, catchers with a dead outlet, idle robots docked there, short power grids). Run it round a base after building or changing it, or from a script on a timer.
params: A world point (the moon's centre is 0,0,0; its surface is about 2000 m out)
Radius in metres round the point
notes: Problem shapes: `machines` `{id, kind, status, flow, power}`; `catchers` `{id, kg, full, outlet}`; `robots` `{dock, number, status, kg}`; `shortGrids` `{id, machines, satisfaction, supplyKw, demandKw, storedKwh}`.
`here`: what's within the radius. `ok` is true when `problems` is 0.

/robots.about: Every J.O.O.N.A.S. robot from the game's robot map: its dock, number, owner, status text, position, kilograms carried, bin size and the dust region under it.
/robots.use: Find where every J.O.O.N.A.S. is, what it's doing ("Cleaning Sector 14933", "No dusty sector found nearby"), and how full its bin is: robots that ran out of nearby dust need moving.

/structures/check.about: Ask the game whether a structure could be placed: its own placement check, the one the build tool's blue preview waits for. Builds nothing.
/structures/check.use: Before building anything from a script, ask the game whether it fits: the same check as the build tool's blue preview. Nothing is spent and nothing changes, so a script can try positions until one fits.
body: Where it goes, in world coordinates
The id of the structure it stands on (a floor or post); -1 for the ground
The build tool's own flags: on a raised floor, free placement, snapped to a grid
The build tool's placement hint, if any
errors: `"ok": false` with the game's `reason` (for example something in the way, or too steep)
notes: A POST because it carries a body, but it changes nothing: it works without `allow-writes`.
`multiLevel`: whether the game's stacking check accepts it (floors on posts, and so on).

/structures/create.about: Build a structure with the game's own `TryBuildStructure`: the same check, then built and paid for like the build tool would.
/structures/create.use: Build a structure from a script: floors, posts, machines, catchers, robots. The game checks and charges it exactly as if you'd placed it by hand. Move the player within 22 m first (`/player/modify`), then confirm with `/structures?since=`.
body: Where it goes, in world coordinates
The id of the structure it stands on (a floor or post); -1 for the ground
The build tool's own flags: on a raised floor, free placement, snapped to a grid
The build tool's placement hint, if any
notes: The player must be within about 22 m: move them first with `POST /player/modify`.
Check with `/structures/check` first; `GET /structures?since=<id>` shows what was just built.

/structures/remove.about: Take structures out of the world from anywhere, without moving the player. The game's normal refund is paid into the team's money unless `refund=0`.
/structures/remove.use: Take down structures from anywhere on the moon with the normal refund: clearing an old base, undoing a script's mistake. Remove one at a time, about a quarter of a second apart, or the game freezes.
params: `1`: J.O.O.N.A.S. robots (kind 99) may be removed too
notes: **Remove one at a time with about 0.25 s between.** The game's removal costs about 15 ms after a pause but 100-130 ms straight after another; a batch freezes the game.
`skipped`: robots left because `robot=1` wasn't given. `missing`: ids that weren't there. `ok` is false when anything asked for is still standing.

/belts/check.about: Ask the game whether a belt can be built between two points: whether it's routable, its length and its price. Builds nothing.
/belts/check.use: Before laying a belt from a script, ask whether the game will accept that route, how long it is and what it costs. Use `/kit` for the limits (longest belt, tightest turn, steepest slope).
body: Where the belt starts and ends
The machine or catcher port it connects to at each end, by structure id
The belt it continues from or into, by belt id
The up direction at each end
notes: Works without `allow-writes`: it changes nothing.
`price` is a string (the game's decimal). `/kit` has the limits: length, radius, slope, height.

/belts/create.about: Build a belt with the game's own `TryBuildConveyor`, paid for like the build tool would.
/belts/create.use: Lay a belt between two points or two machines' ports from a script, paid for as by hand. Connect it to machines with `startStructure` / `endStructure`.
body: Where the belt starts and ends
The machine or catcher port it connects to at each end, by structure id
The belt it continues from or into, by belt id
The up direction at each end
notes: The player must be within about 22 m: move them first with `POST /player/modify`.

/belts/remove.about: Take belts out with the game's own undo, from anywhere; the game refunds them itself.
/belts/remove.use: Remove belts from anywhere, refunded: rerouting a line, or clearing up after a test.
notes: `refund`: how much the team's money went up.

/canisters/remove.about: Delete one loose capsule lying on the ground.
/canisters/remove.use: Delete a stray capsule lying on the ground, for example one that fell off a belt and blocks a path.
errors: `{"ok":false,"reason":"canister is riding, carried or flying"}`: only loose ones can go

/builder.about: The player's own build tool: whether it's placing, the kind on it, whether the preview is valid and why not, its placement plan, and what overlaps the preview.
/builder.use: See what the player's own build tool is showing: the piece it's placing, whether the preview is valid, and if not, the game's reason and what it overlaps. The way to understand why a placement is refused.
notes: `overlaps`: every collider in a foundation-sized box at the preview, which is what "overlaps another tile" means.

/builder/aim.about: Pick a structure kind on the real build tool and aim it along a ray, as the camera would; the game then makes its own placement preview (stacking included).
/builder/aim.use: Drive the real build tool from a script: choose a piece and point it, and the game makes its own preview, stacking on floors and posts included. Useful when you want exactly what a player would get, rather than `/structures/create`'s direct placement.
body: The aim ray: from a point towards another
The rotate wheel, as the mouse wheel turns it
notes: Then `POST /builder/place` presses place; `GET /builder` shows whether the preview is valid first.

/builder/place.about: Press place on the build tool, as aimed by `/builder/aim`.
/builder/place.use: Press "place" on the build tool after `/builder/aim`, as a player clicking.

/builder/stop.about: Put the build tool down and cancel any placement.
/builder/stop.use: Put the build tool away again after a script used it.

/player.about: The local player: position, facing, pitch, heading and where the camera looks.
/player.use: Where the player is and which way they look: a script's starting point for building near them, or for putting the observer camera behind them.

/player/modify.about: Move the local player with the game's own teleport. They land on the surface above the point.
/player/modify.use: Move the player anywhere on the moon. Scripts use it to stand within building reach (about 22 m) of where they build next; it's also a quick way to reach a far base.
params: A world point (the moon's centre is 0,0,0; its surface is about 2000 m out)
notes: Ignored while the player is in a vehicle.
Building needs the player within about 22 m; removing doesn't.

/camera.about: Which camera draws: the game's, or the observer camera with where it is and where it looks.
/camera.use: Find out whether the observer camera is on and where it is.
notes: With the observer camera on: `{"camera":"observer","pos":[...],"forward":[...]}`.

/camera/modify.about: Put an observer camera somewhere, looking at a point: a second camera drawn on top of the game's, which stays where it's put while the player moves (for recording). The game's look-at cards are hidden while it's on.
/camera/modify.use: **Film or watch from a fixed angle.** An observer camera stays where you put it while the player walks about, so a script can build a base with the player running from spot to spot and the picture stays steady: for recording a timelapse, watching a long build, or a screenshot from the sky. `hide=1` stops the game's own camera drawing underneath, which is cheaper. The game's info cards stay hidden while it's on.
params: `1`: the game's own camera stops drawing underneath (cheaper)

/camera/remove.about: Remove the observer camera and give the view back to the game's camera.
/camera/remove.use: Give the view back to the game's own camera when you're done filming or watching.

/message.about: Show a line of text on screen, in the game's font (for a script's status while it builds). Empty text hides it.
/message.use: Show a script's progress on screen in the game's own font ("Building row 3 of 12"), so you can follow a long job while playing or recording. Empty text hides it; `ttl` takes it down by itself.
params: The text; empty hides the message
Seconds it stays up; 0 until replaced
Height on screen, 0 bottom to 1 top

/clean.about: Run the game's own `CleanAt` round a point: clears dust there, as the player's sweeping does.
/clean.use: Clear dust round a point without walking there, exactly as the player's sweeping does: tidying a build site, or clearing a path for belts.
params: A world point (the moon's centre is 0,0,0; its surface is about 2000 m out)
notes: `returned`: what the game's `CleanAt` returned.

/game/money.use: Read the team's money from a script, for example to stop a build script before it runs out.

/debug/threads.about: Every thread of the game's process as the system sees it: id, state, CPU seconds used and when it started. For a game that hangs but still answers.
/debug/threads.use: When the game hangs but still answers, see which threads are busy and which started late: a first step in finding a freeze.
notes: Threads that started late (when quitting, say) or keep using CPU are the ones to look at.

/lobby.about: What your hosted game publishes to Steam: whether you're in a lobby and host, the crew name, privacy, the lobby id and every lobby key.
/lobby.use: See exactly what your hosted game publishes to Steam's server list: the crew name, privacy and every lobby key.

/lobby/modify.about: Set your hosted game's name in the server list (the game has no box for it), or set one lobby key directly. Host only.
/lobby/modify.use: Give your hosted game a proper name in the server list (the game has no box to type one), or set a lobby key directly.
params: The new crew name, 1-60 characters. Changes the game's field, every lobby key that held the old name, then refreshes the lobby
Instead of `name`: set one lobby key

/vehicles.about: Every owned vehicle (storage id, owner, garage, type, whether it's out in the world, price), the garage's offers, and the team's money.
/vehicles.use: See every vehicle the crew owns, who owns it, whether it's out in the world, and what each would refund.

/vehicles/remove.about: Take one owned vehicle away (out of the world if it's out); with `refund=1` its garage price is paid to the team.
/vehicles/remove.use: Take away a vehicle (a crew-mate's who left, or one stuck somewhere), optionally refunding its price to the team.
params: The vehicle's storage id, as `/vehicles` lists it
`1`: pay its garage price to the team
errors: `{"ok":false,"reason":"no owned vehicle with that storage id"}`

/dev/find.about: Find game methods by name: every class in the game's code with a method of that name, whether it's static or public, its parameters and return type, and how many live objects of the class there are.
/dev/find.use: For modders: find which game class has a method you've heard of, and how many live objects of it exist, before patching or calling it.
notes: `live`: -1 for a static method or a class that isn't a Unity object.

/dev/xref.about: Find game methods whose code uses a string containing some text: a cross-reference search through the game's machine code.
/dev/xref.use: For modders: find the code behind a message you see in the game or the log, by searching the game's code for the text ("looked clean" leads to the start-up dust check).
params: Only this class (full name, for example `MoonCleaners.MoonWorld`)
notes: Without `type` it scans every method in the game, which takes a while.

/dev/dis.about: Disassemble a game method: its machine code, with the strings it uses and the methods it calls named. Answers in plain text.
/dev/dis.use: For modders: read what a game method actually does, as machine code with the strings it uses and the methods it calls named. The way to understand a game system with no source.
params: Which overload, when there are several
/dev/dis.answer:
== MoonCleaners.MoonWorld::StepProduction/1 @ 0x6FFFF7850D10
0000  mov rax,rsp
0003  push rbx
0004  push rsi
...
00D0  call 00006FFFF7844AC0h                          -> MoonCleaners.MoonWorld::SolvePower/1
01B6  call 00006FFFF78194D0h                          -> MoonCleaners.MoonWorld::Processor/1
...
errors: `{"ok":false,"reason":"no such method (2 overloads)"}`: `n` is past the last overload

/dev/fields.about: A class's fields with their memory offsets, in plain text.
/dev/fields.use: For modders: list a class's fields with their memory offsets, to read or patch game state.

/dev/name.about: Which known game method contains a code address, for reading a crash or a stack.
/dev/name.use: For modders: turn a code address from a crash or a stack trace into the game method it's in.
notes: `exact: true` with `name` when the address is a method's start.

/dev/call.about: Call a game method that takes no parameters: a static one, or on every live object of its class. For the game's own developer tools; nothing runs unless asked.
/dev/call.use: For modders: run one of the game's own parameterless methods on purpose, such as a developer reset hidden in the game. Use with care: it does whatever that method does.
errors: `"ok": false` with the exception it threw
notes: A static method answers `{"ok":true,"static":true,"returned":...}`.

/help.about: Every endpoint there is right now, described by whoever serves it: the core's, each module's by area, and each plugin's `HttpHelp()` lines, hot or normal. LunarLink's own come with these details.
/help.use: Discover what this game can do right now: every endpoint, LunarLink's and every plugin's, grouped by area. `?details=1` adds parameters, examples and these notes, so a script or tool can build itself from it.
params: Only endpoints whose path starts with this

/help.html.about: The same list as a searchable page, with these details: open it in a browser.
/help.html.use: The searchable reference with everything installed in your game, plugins' endpoints included: open it in a browser while you play.

/plugins.about: The normal BepInEx plugins in `BepInEx/plugins/`: name, GUID, version, file, state and which other plugins need each one.
/plugins.use: See which normal BepInEx plugins are installed, their versions, which are on, and which depend on which: the same list as F9's BEPINEX PLUGINS tab, for a script.
notes: `state`: `running`, `off from next start`, `off`, or `on from next start`.
`file` is what `/plugins/disable` and `/plugins/enable` take.

/plugins/disable.about: Turn a normal BepInEx plugin off from the next game start, by renaming its DLL to `.dll.disabled`. A loaded plugin keeps running until the restart.
/plugins/disable.use: Switch a mod off for the next game start without hunting for its DLL in the folders, for example to test whether a mod causes a problem. Restart to apply.
params: The plugin's file as `/plugins` lists it, for example `QuantumConveyors/QuantumConveyors.dll`
errors: `"ok": false` with a `reason`: no such plugin, it's already off, another plugin needs it (`... is needed by ...: turn those off first`), or it's LunarLink itself

/plugins/enable.about: Turn a normal BepInEx plugin back on from the next game start (renames `.dll.disabled` back). Turning one back on before restarting needs no restart.
/plugins/enable.use: Switch a mod back on for the next start. Turning back on one you switched off this session needs no restart at all.
params: The plugin's file as `/plugins` lists it
errors: `"ok": false` with a `reason`: it's already on, or there's no `.dll.disabled` file

/perf.about: fps and milliseconds per frame since the last read: of the timed systems (`msPerFrame`), and with the engine counters on, Unity's own (`engineMs`).
/perf.use: Read where the frame time goes: fps, Unity's own counters (scripts, physics, rendering, GPU wait) and any timers you put in. Read once, wait 10-20 s, read again.

/perf/engine.about: Turn Unity's own frame counters on or off: whole frame, scripts, physics, rendering, GPU wait, draw calls. They cost almost nothing.
/perf/engine.use: Turn on Unity's own frame counters, the lightest way to measure (almost free). Turn them off when done.

/perf/timers.about: Stopwatches on the game's and MoonFramework's main per-frame systems, read through `/perf`.
/perf/timers.use: Time the game's and MoonFramework's main systems each frame, to find which one is slow on a big base. They cost frame time themselves: reload the Perf module to take them out.
notes: They patch the game and cost frame time: take them out with `POST /hot/reload?name=LunarLink.Perf` (or turn the module off).

/perf/time.about: A stopwatch on one method, read through `/perf`.
/perf/time.use: Time one particular method you suspect (`/perf/methods` lists them), read through `/perf`.
errors: `"ok": false` with `no type ...` or `no method ... in it or its parents`
notes: Answers `{"ok":true,"already":true}` when it's already timed.

/perf/methods.about: The methods a class declares, as `Name/paramCount`, to pick one to time.
/perf/methods.use: List a class's methods, to pick one for `/perf/time`.

/census.about: Every component in the scene counted by class, with which classes have per-frame methods. Where the frame might be going.
/census.use: Count every component in the scene by class: shows what there's thousands of (belts, lights, machines) and which run code every frame.
params: How many classes to list, most common first

/update.about: What LunarLink's updater knows: the running version, the latest release (after `/update/check`), its notes, how far an update got, and each module in the module channel. Nothing here contacts GitHub.
/update.use: What's installed and what's newer: LunarLink's release, each module, each plugin with updates. For a script or an overlay that tells you when to update.
/update.answer:
{
 "ok": true,
 "running": "0.3.0",
 "state": "up to date",
 "latest": "0.3.0",
 "page": "https://github.com/swheettaos/lunarlink/releases/tag/v0.3.0",
 "size": 132053,
 "coreChanged": null,
 "detail": "LunarLink 0.3.0 is the latest release",
 "error": null,
 "notes": "- **Module channel.** Every push to main is built on GitHub ...",
 "channel": {
  "error": null,
  "modules": [
   {
    "name": "LunarLink.Api",
    "state": "up to date",
    "note": "Api: /dev/dis reads small ?bytes= too (below 256 it read nothing)",
    "built": "2026-11-14 00:56:10 UTC",
    "commit": "83eaf7ae3a7c",
    "size": 147968,
    "error": null
   },
   {
    "name": "LunarLink.Perf",
    "state": "up to date",
    "note": "Perf: reach MoonFramework by name, so LunarLink no longer builds against it",
    "built": "2026-11-14 00:52:40 UTC",
    "commit": "5ac09763a51f",
    "size": 32768,
    "error": null
   },
   {
    "name": "LunarLink.Window",
    "state": "up to date",
    "note": "Module channel: CI publishes changed modules; F9 offers each one and reloads it in place",
    "built": "2026-11-14 00:52:40 UTC",
    "commit": "fe46c3faccb3",
    "size": 28672,
    "error": null
   }
  ]
 }
}
notes: `state` (the release): `idle`, `checking`, `up to date`, `available`, `downloading`, `reloading`, `done` (modules reloaded, no restart), `restart` (a new core is in place: restart the game) or `failed` (see `error`).
`coreChanged`: known once a release is downloaded: `false` means its modules reloaded in place, `true` that the core changed and the game needs a restart.

`channel.modules[].state`: `up to date`, `available` (a newer build from main), `needs core` (built for a newer core: install the next release first), `downloading`, `reloading`, `updated` or `failed`.
`autoCheck`: whether it checks by itself once at every game start (`POST /update/modify?auto=`).

`plugins`: each plugin that answers `UpdateFeed()`: `name`, `kind` (`hot` or `plugin`), `version`, `latest`, `state` (`checking`, `up to date`, `available`, `downloading`, `reloading`, `updated`, `restart`, `failed`), `from` (where it comes from), `notes`, `error`.
The F9 window's UPDATES tab shows the same, with Check for updates and an Update button on each row.

/update/modify.about: Turn "check for updates at game start" on or off: when on, LunarLink checks GitHub once by itself at every game start, after the moon loads (not on module reloads). Off by default: checking is manual. It's the checkbox on F9's UPDATES tab.
/update/modify.use: Have LunarLink check for updates by itself at every game start (off by default).
notes: Kept in `BepInEx/plugins/LunarLink/update_auto.txt`. It only checks: nothing is installed until you press Update.

/update/check.about: Ask GitHub for LunarLink's latest release and the module channel's `modules.json`, in the background; read `GET /update` for the answer. LunarLink never checks by itself: only this request (or F9's button) contacts GitHub, and once after a core update you started, when the game is back.
/update/check.use: Ask GitHub for news (the latest release, module builds, plugins' feeds), then read `/update`.
/update/check.answer: {"ok": true, "running": "0.3.0", "state": "checking", "latest": null, "page": null, "size": 0, "coreChanged": null, "detail": null, "error": null, "notes": null, "channel": {"error": null, "modules": []}}
notes: A POST because it starts something, but it changes nothing in the game: it works without `allow-writes`.
It asks `api.github.com/repos/swheettaos/lunarlink/releases/latest` and downloads the `modules` prerelease's `modules.json`, with only a generic `LunarLink-updater` user agent.

/update/apply.about: Install an update. Without `module`: the latest release. Its zip is checked against the SHA-256 GitHub publishes; if the core didn't change, the modules go into `BepInEx/hot/` and reload in place, and if it did, the new core replaces the running one for the next start (the running file is renamed to `LunarLink.dll.old`) and the modules wait until then. With `module`: that module's newer build from the module channel, checked against `modules.json`'s SHA-256 and reloaded in place.
/update/apply.use: Install an update from a script: a release, one module or all, or a plugin. Modules and hot plugins reload in place; only a new core needs a restart.
params: A module's name (`LunarLink.Api`), or `all`: every module with a newer build. Only builds made for the installed core are taken
A plugin's name, as `GET /update` lists it under `plugins`: its own update, from where its `UpdateFeed()` says
Without `module`: install the latest release even when it's the version already running (a repair)
/update/apply.answer: {"ok": true, "running": "0.3.0", "state": "up to date", "...": "...", "channel": {"error": null, "modules": [{"name": "LunarLink.Api", "state": "downloading", "note": "Api: /structures answers kinds by name too", "built": "2026-11-14 01:02:11 UTC", "commit": "3f1c2a9d0b4e", "size": 145920, "error": null}]}}
errors: `{"ok":false,"reason":"LunarLink.Api is built for a newer core: install the next LunarLink release first"}`

`state: failed` (release) or a module's `state: failed` in `GET /update`, with the reason in `error`: the download didn't match its SHA-256, the zip didn't hold LunarLink's files, or a module failed to start. Nothing is installed when the check fails.
notes: It runs in the background: follow it with `GET /update` until the release's `state` is `done` or `restart`, or the module's is `updated`.
Only LunarLink's own files are taken from a release zip (`BepInEx/plugins/LunarLink/*` and `BepInEx/hot/LunarLink.*.dll`).
A module you turned off stays off; it loads the new build when you turn it on.
After a core update, the game checks once more when it's back, so module builds newer than that release are offered.
